models.best: Inferred from its principle that goods move as gifts creating obligations to return, so credit can rest on trust among known households rather than on a central issuer. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that gifts bind givers and receivers to return favours, so a debt of obligation can pass down a family and outsiders who lack a known giver have no credit at all. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Mauss, The Gift; Sahlins, Stone Age Economics

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a family farm balances its work against household needs, so it borrows only to meet those needs and avoids debt taken on to chase profit. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that production serves consumption, so when harvests fail a household with no savings must borrow at high cost and may lose its land to creditors. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Chayanov, The Theory of Peasant Economy

models.best: Inferred from its principle that tribute and taxes are stored at the centre and paid out to officials and workers, so pay and rations hold steady through poor harvests. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the centre controls both collection and payment, so pay and rations can be withheld from officials or workers who fall out of favour, and the stored surplus can serve the ruler's own ends. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Polanyi, The Great Transformation; Polanyi, Arensberg and Pearson, Trade and Market in the Early Empires

models.best: Inferred from its principle that output is sold through trade, so merchants extend credit against produce and settle accounts in bills, which speeds trade among owners. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that labour is extracted through the ownership of people, so enslaved people are denied property and any way to save or borrow, and the value of their work is captured by owners' credit. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Williams, Capitalism and Slavery

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the manor is largely self-supplying, so less money is needed and dues paid in kind keep food and goods moving in hard times. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that peasants owe labour services and rents to a lord, so cash stays scarce, debts are bound to the land, and tenants cannot easily borrow elsewhere or leave. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Bloch, Feudal Society; Capitulare de villis

models.best: Inferred from its principle that guild statutes regulate entry, training, quality and prices, so masters keep standards steady and apprentices train under agreed rules. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that guilds regulate entry and prices, so newcomers are shut out of a trade, credit is controlled by masters, and prices stay high even when demand falls. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Boileau, Le Livre des métiers; Epstein, Freedom and Growth

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the state seeks a trade surplus and gold, so it keeps specie in the realm and aims to keep the money supply in step with trade. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that surpluses and colonies are sought by regulation, so the state hoards bullion, restricts the money in circulation and penalises the export of gold, which squeezes trade. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Mun, England's Treasure by Forraign Trade; Heckscher, Mercantilism

models.best: Inferred from its principle that wealth is the net product of the land, so money should follow real output and the state should fund itself by a single tax on land rent rather than by issuing money. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that only agriculture is productive, so a state that taxes only land rent may starve credit and manufacture, and money issued against trade in goods is distrusted. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Quesnay, Tableau économique; Meek, The Economics of Physiocracy

models.best: Inferred from its principle that competitive markets and private property allocate capital well, so note issue and lending are left to competing private banks bound by contract. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state protects property and contracts and otherwise stays out, so with no lender of last resort a run on one bank can spread to sound banks, and credit can freeze across the economy. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Smith, The Wealth of Nations

models.best: Competition in note issue, as in Scottish free banking and its end: a World Bank paper dates it from 1716 but argues that reforms of those years made it a cartel. Rockoff's working paper reports a wave of notes under £1 from banks and individual merchants. The 19th-century end is thinly covered, and sources disagree on the rules and on whether it was truly free banking.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that credit expansion distorts production, so when cheap credit ends, firms that borrowed against it must liquidate, and a bust can spread through the banks. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Menger, Grundsätze der Volkswirthschaftslehre; Hayek, The Use of Knowledge in Society

models.best: Estonia's kroon and its currency board: a country studies website credits the June 1992 kroon with much of the stabilisation that followed. The sources are short summaries, give no peg rate, and agree on inflation only in broad terms.
models.worst: Estonia's kroon and its currency board: an IMF working paper of 2002 warns that, without a fast drop in inflation, thin reserves would be spent defending an unrealistic exchange rate. The sources are short summaries, and the inflation figures agree only in broad terms. Source: Eesti Pank (Bank of Estonia), history page (year not shown in the search result); country studies website on Estonia (publisher and year not shown in the search result); Deutsche Bundesbank keynote on 30 years of monetary reform in Estonia (2022); IMF working paper 'The Estonian Currency Board' (2002); IMF Staff Papers, 'The Operation of the Estonian Currency Board' (1993)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that public spending rises in slumps and falls in booms, so a central bank that eases credit in recessions and tightens in booms keeps demand and employment high. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that spending and taxes must move against the cycle, so a state that keeps deficits and easy money after a boom may let inflation build while the money stock outruns output. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Keynes, The General Theory; Beveridge, Social Insurance and Allied Services

models.best: Bundesbank independence under the 1957 statute: section 12 declares the bank independent of Federal Government instructions when it uses its statutory powers, as an ECB working paper quotes it, not the full text. Sources say parliament could amend or abolish the bank by ordinary law. The bank's claim of the lowest G7 inflation from 1956 to 1998 is its own self-assessment.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a legal order must curb monopoly, so credit left to a cartel of banks can favour incumbent firms and shut out newcomers, with its costs falling on borrowers. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Müller-Armack, Wirtschaftslenkung und Marktwirtschaft; Erhard, Wohlstand für Alle

models.best: Inferred from its principle that national wage bargaining sets pay across the economy, so wage settlements are coordinated with monetary policy and inflation stays low without sharp rate shocks. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that wages are set nationally, so a settlement that outruns productivity can push up prices and force the central bank into tight money that costs jobs. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Saltsjöbaden Agreement; Esping-Andersen, The Three Worlds of Welfare Capitalism

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the state directs credit and export targets to chosen industries, so state lenders and the central bank steer money to firms that meet performance targets. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that credit is steered by the state, so loans can keep flowing to firms that miss their targets for years, and the banking system can carry their losses. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Johnson, MITI and the Japanese Miracle; Amsden, Asia's Next Giant

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the rent of land funds public services, so money and credit stay with productive activity and banks lend less against land speculation. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that land is taxed rather than labour and capital, so where rent taxes are weak, credit flows into property and banks lend against inflated land values, which can end in a bust. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: George, Progress and Poverty

models.best: Inferred from its principle that cooperative communities built by example replace private profit, so small community funds lend to members at cost as the communities grow. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that association is voluntary and built by example, so a community credit fund that relies on trust can collapse when a few members default and no common reserve stands behind it. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Owen, A New View of Society; Fourier, Le Nouveau Monde industriel

models.best: Inferred from its principle that mutual credit lets banks lend at cost and workers keep the full value of their work, so money is issued against real exchange and rent on property is removed. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that free mutual contracts run without a state, so credit not backed by a common reserve can lose value in a run, and the holders of mutual notes bear the loss. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Proudhon, What Is Property?

models.best: Inferred from its principle that members own and control banks on one member one vote, so surplus is shared between users and workers and loans serve members' needs. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that one member one vote governs the bank, so decisions on lending can favour members' own projects, and outside capital cannot step in to correct weak decisions, which leaves depositors exposed. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Rochdale Society of Equitable Pioneers; Mondragón cooperatives

models.best: Inferred from its principle that goods are shared by need within federated communes, so no wages or money are created to pay for them, and credit is given as mutual aid. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that there is no state and no wages, so a commune that runs short of goods has no common reserve or authority to issue money or raise credit to cover the gap. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kropotkin, The Conquest of Bread

models.best: Inferred from its principle that trade unions run industry through workers' organisations, so strike funds and workers' own banks can finance workers' enterprises. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that industry is run through strikes and eventually a general strike, so a long strike can drain credit from firms and banks, and a general strike can halt payments for everyone. models.best: Inferred from its principle that socialism comes by democratic and gradual means, so a public bank can lend for housing and works under elected control. There is no documented case in the pool.

models.best: Inferred from its principle that workers and consumers share control through guild-like councils, so credit for industry is set by producers and users together, with the state as one partner. There is no documented case in the pool.

models.best: Inferred from its principle that central plans set investment, so the state's credit is allocated to the sectors the plan names, which allows fast funding of heavy industry. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: China's central bank separated from the state lenders: the credit plan kept after 1984 assigned quotas to each bank and directed financing to firms, and an IMF article of March 1996 contends that this had an inherent expansionary bias weakening the central bank's control. Source: People's Bank of China, 'A Brief History of the People's Bank of China' (year not shown in the search result); IMF, Finance and Development, March 1996, 'Financial Sector Reforms in China'

compromise.summary: An independent central bank, bound by statute to a published rule for money growth or price stability and barred from lending directly to the state. Note and deposit issue stay open to competing banks, and entry rules are reviewed so that cartels cannot form.
compromise.details: Keeps: Estonia's kroon and its currency board from Monetarist neoliberalism, on thin sources; statutory independence from Social market economy, as in Bundesbank independence under the 1957 statute, which ordinary law could amend; open competition in note issue from Austrian free-market economics, as in Scottish free banking and its end, thinly covered and said to have become a cartel. Blocks: central bank lending to government, with a legal ban on direct monetary finance, as excerpts on German hyperinflation of 1923 suggest; quota credit set by plan, with a legal cap on central bank credit to any one bank, as China's central bank separated from the state lenders suggests; a fixed peg adopted before inflation falls, with a reserve test first; cartel-style entry rules, with a periodic open-entry review. Test: inflation, central bank lending to government and the number of issuing banks, measured yearly over a full economic cycle. Source: pool sources of these cases; Kelton, The Deficit Myth, for the inferred principle that inflation, not debt, is the limit.
